newsitem.title: GERMANY: German union chief urges assault on joblessness.
newsitem.headline: German union chief urges assault on joblessness.

text.p: Germany's top union official on Tuesday urged employers and government to work with the trade unions to reduce unemployment and warned of serious consequences if the attempt failed.

Opening a two-day jobs conference in Berlin, German Trade Union Federation (DGB) chairman Dieter Schulte said Bonn's current policies, including its major tax reform, could lead to Germany being ruled out of the single European currency in 1999.

"The complete removal of the means tax and lower corporate taxes, together with increased expenditure linked to greater joblessness and poverty, will lead to a rise in deficits up to the year 2000," Schulte said in a pre-released text of the speech.

Bonn's official estimate is that its state deficit will falll to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product by the year-end, just under the three percent ceiling targeted in the Maastricht treaty for economic and monetary union.
Referring to the failure of the government-sponsored "Alliance for Jobs" just over a year ago, Schulte said that government and business had missed a "great chance for cooperation" on job creation.

Trade unions last year walked away from the jobs pact, which was designed to link job creation with modest wage demands, when the extent of the spending cuts in Bonn's current austerity package started to become known.
But, hinting that the DGB and its member trade unions would be ready for a second attempt at cooperation with employers and politicians, Schulte said that a mood of "give and take" was now required.
"People must be able to feel that we are behaving honestly with each other," he said.

Investment in jobs-creating areas such as research and technology must not suffer as a result of state spending cuts, he urged, while he joined the calls of employer groups in demanding that non-wage costs be reduced.
He further attacked those politicians calling for a big reduction in the so-called "solidarity tax" that finances the reconstruction of the former Communist-controlled eastern states.
He said the east, with its relatively higher joblessness, required "special support for the foreseeable future".

Schulte said the summit, at which politicians, union leaders and employers will discuss solutions to Germany's unemployment problem, must come up with results that would meet the "high expectations" surrounding it.
